\\(L=\\begin{bmatrix}2\u00260\\\\1\u00261.4142\\end{bmatrix}\\).\n\n---\n\n## 4) QR decomposition\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nOrthogonal \\(Q\\), upper triangular \\(R\\): \\(A=QR\\), \\(Q^TQ=I\\).  \nClassical Gram–Schmidt:\n$$\nv_k=a_k-\\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}(q_j^Ta_k)q_j,\\quad q_k=\\frac{v_k}{\\|v_k\\|}\n$$\nThen \\(R_{jk}=q_j^Ta_k\\).\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef qr_gram_schmidt(A):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    m, n = A.shape\n    Q = np.zeros((m, n))\n    R = np.zeros((n, n))\n    for k in range(n):\n        v = A[:, k].copy()\n        for j in range(k):\n            R[j, k] = np.dot(Q[:, j], A[:, k])\n            v = v - R[j, k] * Q[:, j]\n        R[k, k] = np.linalg.norm(v)\n        if R[k, k] \u003C 1e-15:\n            raise ValueError(\u0022Linearly dependent columns.\u0022)\n        Q[:, k] = v / R[k, k]\n    return Q, R\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}1\u00261\\\\1\u00260\\\\0\u00261\\end{bmatrix}\\).  \n\\(a_1=(1,1,0)^T\\), \\(\\|a_1\\|=\\sqrt2\\), \\(q_1=(1/\\sqrt2,1/\\sqrt2,0)\\).  \n\\(R_{12}=q_1^Ta_2=(1/\\sqrt2)\\cdot1\u002B(1/\\sqrt2)\\cdot0=1/\\sqrt2\\).  \n\\(v_2=a_2-R_{12}q_1=(1,0,1)-(1/\\sqrt2)(1/\\sqrt2,1/\\sqrt2,0)=(1-1/2,-1/2,1)=(0.5,-0.5,1)\\).  \n\\(\\|v_2\\|=\\sqrt{0.25\u002B0.25\u002B1}= \\sqrt1.5\\).  \nSo \\(q_2=v_2/\\sqrt1.5\\).\n\n---\n\n## 5) SVD\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nSingular value decomposition:\n$$\nA=U\\Sigma V^T\n$$\nwhere \\(U,V\\) orthogonal, \\(\\Sigma=\\mathrm{diag}(\\sigma_1\\ge\\cdots\\ge 0)\\).  \nConnection:\n$$\nA^TA = V\\Sigma^2 V^T,\\quad AA^T = U\\Sigma^2 U^T\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef svd_decomposition(A):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)\n    Sigma = np.diag(s)\n    return U, Sigma, Vt\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}3\u00260\\\\4\u00260\\end{bmatrix}\\).  \n\\(A^TA=\\begin{bmatrix}25\u00260\\\\0\u00260\\end{bmatrix}\\Rightarrow \\sigma_1=\\sqrt{25}=5,\\sigma_2=0\\).  \n\\(v_1=(1,0)^T\\).  \nThen \\(u_1=\\frac{Av_1}{\\sigma_1}=\\frac{(3,4)^T}{5}=(0.6,0.8)^T\\).  \nSo \\(A=u_1[5]v_1^T\\).\n\n---\n\n## 6) Eigenvalue decomposition\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFor diagonalizable \\(A\\):\n$$\nA = V\\Lambda V^{-1},\\quad \\Lambda=\\mathrm{diag}(\\lambda_i)\n$$\nEigenpairs satisfy:\n$$\nA v_i = \\lambda_i v_i\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef eigen_decomposition(A):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    w, V = np.linalg.eig(A)\n    Lam = np.diag(w)\n    Vinv = np.linalg.inv(V)\n    return V, Lam, Vinv\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}2\u00261\\\\1\u00262\\end{bmatrix}\\).  \nCharacteristic: \\(\\det(A-\\lambda I)=(2-\\lambda)^2-1=\\lambda^2-4\\lambda\u002B3=0\\).  \n\\(\\lambda=3,1\\).  \nFor \\(\\lambda=3\\): \\((A-3I)v=0\\Rightarrow \\begin{bmatrix}-1\u00261\\\\1\u0026-1\\end{bmatrix}v=0\\Rightarrow v=(1,1)\\).  \nFor \\(\\lambda=1\\): \\(v=(1,-1)\\).\n\n---\n\n## 7) Power iteration\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFor dominant eigenpair \\((\\lambda_{\\max},v)\\):\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=\\frac{Ax_k}{\\|Ax_k\\|},\\quad\n\\lambda_k=\\frac{x_k^TAx_k}{x_k^Tx_k}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef power_iteration(A, x0=None, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-10):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    x = np.ones(n) if x0 is None else _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n    x = x / np.linalg.norm(x)\n\n    lam_old = 0.0\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        y = A @ x\n        x = y / np.linalg.norm(y)\n        lam = float(x.T @ (A @ x))\n        if abs(lam - lam_old) \u003C tol:\n            break\n        lam_old = lam\n    return lam, x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}2\u00261\\\\1\u00262\\end{bmatrix}\\), \\(x_0=(1,0)\\).  \n\\(y_1=Ax_0=(2,1)\\), \\(\\|y_1\\|=\\sqrt5\\), \\(x_1=(2/\\sqrt5,1/\\sqrt5)\\).  \nRayleigh: \\(\\lambda_1=x_1^TAx_1=3 - \\frac{2}{5}=2.6\\) (intermediate value).  \nNext iteration increases toward \\(3\\).\n\n---\n\n## 8) Jacobi iteration\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nSplit \\(A=D\u002BL\u002BU\\) (D diagonal). Jacobi:\n$$\nx^{(k\u002B1)} = D^{-1}\\bigl(b-(L\u002BU)x^{(k)}\\bigr)\n$$\nComponent form:\n$$\nx_i^{(k\u002B1)}=\\frac{1}{a_{ii}}\\left(b_i-\\sum_{j\\ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef jacobi_iteration(A, b, x0=None, max_iter=500, tol=1e-10):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    x = np.zeros(n) if x0 is None else _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n\n    D = np.diag(A)\n    R = A - np.diagflat(D)\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        x_new = (b - R @ x) / D\n        if _norm_inf(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x = x_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSolve:\n\\(\\;10x\u002By=11,\\; x\u002B10y=11\\). Start \\(x^{(0)}=(0,0)\\).  \n\\(x_1^{(1)}=(11-0)/10=1.1\\), \\(y^{(1)}=(11-0)/10=1.1\\).  \nNext: \\(x^{(2)}=(11-1.1)/10=0.99\\), \\(y^{(2)}=(11-1.1)/10=0.99\\). Converges to \\((1,1)\\).\n\n---\n\n## 9) Gauss–Seidel method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nUse newest values immediately:\n$$\nx_i^{(k\u002B1)}=\\frac{1}{a_{ii}}\\left(b_i-\\sum_{j\u003Ci}a_{ij}x_j^{(k\u002B1)}-\\sum_{j\u003Ei}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef gauss_seidel(A, b, x0=None, max_iter=500, tol=1e-10):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    x = np.zeros(n) if x0 is None else _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        x_old = x.copy()\n        for i in range(n):\n            s1 = np.dot(A[i, :i], x[:i])\n            s2 = np.dot(A[i, i\u002B1:], x_old[i\u002B1:])\n            x[i] = (b[i] - s1 - s2) / A[i, i]\n        if _norm_inf(x - x_old) \u003C tol:\n            return x\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSame system \\(10x\u002By=11,\\;x\u002B10y=11\\), \\(x^{(0)}=(0,0)\\).  \nIter1: \\(x^{(1)}=(11-0)/10=1.1\\).  \nThen \\(y^{(1)}=(11-1.1)/10=0.99\\).  \nIter2: \\(x^{(2)}=(11-0.99)/10=1.001\\); \\(y^{(2)}=(11-1.001)/10=0.9999\\). Faster than Jacobi.\n\n---\n\n## 10) Conjugate gradient method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nSolve SPD \\(Ax=b\\) minimizing:\n$$\nf(x)=\\frac12 x^TAx-b^Tx,\\quad \\nabla f = Ax-b=-r\n$$\nIteration (common form):\n$$\nr_0=b-Ax_0,\\; p_0=r_0\n$$\n$$\n\\alpha_k=\\frac{r_k^Tr_k}{p_k^TAp_k},\\quad x_{k\u002B1}=x_k\u002B\\alpha_k p_k\n$$\n$$\nr_{k\u002B1}=r_k-\\alpha_kAp_k,\\quad\n\\beta_k=\\frac{r_{k\u002B1}^Tr_{k\u002B1}}{r_k^Tr_k},\\quad\np_{k\u002B1}=r_{k\u002B1}\u002B\\beta_k p_k\n$$\n(See standard derivations and discussions in CG references.) [6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivation_of_the_conjugate_gradient_method)[4](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~quake-papers/painless-conjugate-gradient.pdf)[7](https://web.stanford.edu/class/ee364b/lectures/conj_grad_slides.pdf)\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef conjugate_gradient(A, b, x0=None, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-10):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    x = np.zeros(n) if x0 is None else _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n\n    r = b - A @ x\n    p = r.copy()\n    rs_old = float(r @ r)\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        Ap = A @ p\n        alpha = rs_old / float(p @ Ap)\n        x = x \u002B alpha * p\n        r = r - alpha * Ap\n        rs_new = float(r @ r)\n        if np.sqrt(rs_new) \u003C tol:\n            return x\n        beta = rs_new / rs_old\n        p = r \u002B beta * p\n        rs_old = rs_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}4\u00261\\\\1\u00263\\end{bmatrix}\\), \\(b=(1,2)\\), \\(x_0=(0,0)\\).  \n\\(r_0=b=(1,2)\\), \\(p_0=r_0\\).  \n\\(Ap_0=(4*1\u002B1*2,\\;1*1\u002B3*2)=(6,7)\\).  \n\\(\\alpha_0=(r_0^Tr_0)/(p_0^TAp_0)=(1^2\u002B2^2)/(1*6\u002B2*7)=5/20=0.25\\).  \n\\(x_1=(0,0)\u002B0.25(1,2)=(0.25,0.5)\\).  \n\\(r_1=r_0-\\alpha_0Ap_0=(1,2)-0.25(6,7)=(1-1.5,\\;2-1.75)=(-0.5,0.25)\\).  \nContinue similarly; in exact arithmetic CG solves 2×2 in ≤2 steps.\n\n---\n\n## 11) Least squares fitting\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nGiven \\(A\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m\\times n}\\), minimize \\(\\|Ax-b\\|_2^2\\).  \nNormal equations:\n$$\nA^TAx=A^Tb\n$$\nQR approach (preferred numerically):\n$$\nA=QR,\\quad \\min \\|QRx-b\\| \\Rightarrow Rx=Q^Tb\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef least_squares_qr(A, b):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n    Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A, mode=\u0022reduced\u0022)\n    y = Q.T @ b\n    x = np.linalg.solve(R, y)\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nFit line \\(y\\approx c_0\u002Bc_1x\\) to points \\((0,1),(1,2),(2,2)\\).  \n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}1\u00260\\\\1\u00261\\\\1\u00262\\end{bmatrix}\\), \\(b=(1,2,2)\\).  \nCompute \\(A^TA=\\begin{bmatrix}3\u00263\\\\3\u00265\\end{bmatrix}\\), \\(A^Tb=(5,6)\\).  \nSolve:\n\\(\\begin{bmatrix}3\u00263\\\\3\u00265\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}c_0\\\\c_1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}5\\\\6\\end{bmatrix}\\).  \nEliminate: row2-row1 ⇒ \\(2c_1=1\\Rightarrow c_1=0.5\\).  \nThen \\(3c_0\u002B3*0.5=5\\Rightarrow 3c_0=3.5\\Rightarrow c_0=1.1667\\).\n\n---\n\n# Root Finding\n\n## 12) Bisection method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nIf \\(f(a)f(b)\u003C0\\), root in \\([a,b]\\). Midpoint \\(c=(a\u002Bb)/2\\).  \nShrink interval based on sign:\n$$\n(a,b)\\leftarrow\n\\begin{cases}\n(a,c),\u0026 f(a)f(c)\u003C0\\\\\n(c,b),\u0026 f(c)f(b)\u003C0\n\\end{cases}\n$$\nError bound after \\(n\\) steps:\n$$\n|x^*-c_n|\\le \\frac{b-a}{2^{n\u002B1}}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef bisection(f, a, b, max_iter=200, tol=1e-12):\n    fa, fb = f(a), f(b)\n    if fa * fb \u003E 0:\n        raise ValueError(\u0022f(a) and f(b) must have opposite signs.\u0022)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        c = 0.5 * (a \u002B b)\n        fc = f(c)\n        if abs(fc) \u003C tol or 0.5 * (b - a) \u003C tol:\n            return c\n        if fa * fc \u003C 0:\n            b, fb = c, fc\n        else:\n            a, fa = c, fc\n    return 0.5 * (a \u002B b)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nFind root of \\(f(x)=x^2-2\\) on \\([1,2]\\).  \n\\(f(1)=-1\\), \\(f(2)=2\\).  \n1) \\(c=1.5\\), \\(f(c)=0.25\u003E0\\Rightarrow [1,1.5]\\)  \n2) \\(c=1.25\\), \\(f=-0.4375\u003C0\\Rightarrow [1.25,1.5]\\)  \n3) \\(c=1.375\\), \\(f=-0.109375\u003C0\\Rightarrow [1.375,1.5]\\)  \n4) \\(c=1.4375\\), \\(f=0.06640625\u003E0\\Rightarrow [1.375,1.4375]\\) … converges to \\(\\sqrt2\\).\n\n---\n\n## 13) Newton–Raphson\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nLinearize:\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=x_k-\\frac{f(x_k)}{f\u0027(x_k)}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef newton_raphson(f, df, x0, max_iter=100, tol=1e-12):\n    x = float(x0)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        fx = f(x)\n        dfx = df(x)\n        if abs(dfx) \u003C 1e-15:\n            raise ValueError(\u0022Derivative too small.\u0022)\n        x_new = x - fx / dfx\n        if abs(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x = x_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(f(x)=x^2-2\\), \\(f\u0027(x)=2x\\), start \\(x_0=1.5\\).  \n\\(x_1=1.5-\\frac{0.25}{3}=1.4166667\\).  \n\\(f(x_1)=1.4166667^2-2=0.0069444\\).  \n\\(x_2=1.4166667-\\frac{0.0069444}{2.8333334}=1.4142157\\).\n\n---\n\n## 14) Secant method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nApproximate derivative by secant slope:\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=x_k-f(x_k)\\frac{x_k-x_{k-1}}{f(x_k)-f(x_{k-1})}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef secant(f, x0, x1, max_iter=200, tol=1e-12):\n    x_prev, x = float(x0), float(x1)\n    f_prev, fx = f(x_prev), f(x)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        denom = fx - f_prev\n        if abs(denom) \u003C 1e-15:\n            raise ValueError(\u0022Zero secant slope.\u0022)\n        x_new = x - fx * (x - x_prev) / denom\n        if abs(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x_prev, f_prev = x, fx\n        x, fx = x_new, f(x_new)\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(f(x)=x^2-2\\), \\(x_0=1\\), \\(x_1=2\\).  \n\\(x_2=2-2\\cdot(2-1)/(2-(-1))=2-2/3=1.3333333\\).  \n\\(f(x_2)=-0.2222222\\).  \n\\(x_3=1.3333333-(-0.2222)(1.3333-2)/(-0.2222-2)=1.4\\).\n\n---\n\n## 15) Fixed-point iteration\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nRewrite \\(x=g(x)\\). Iterate:\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=g(x_k)\n$$\nConverges if \\(|g\u0027(x^*)|\u003C1\\) near fixed point.\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef fixed_point(g, x0, max_iter=500, tol=1e-12):\n    x = float(x0)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        x_new = float(g(x))\n        if abs(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x = x_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSolve \\(x=\\cos x\\). Take \\(g(x)=\\cos x\\), \\(x_0=1\\).  \n\\(x_1=\\cos1=0.5403023\\)  \n\\(x_2=\\cos0.5403023=0.8575532\\)  \n\\(x_3=\\cos0.8575532=0.6542898\\) … converges to ~0.739085.\n\n---\n\n## 16) Müller\u0027s method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nQuadratic through \\((x_{k-2},f_{k-2}), (x_{k-1},f_{k-1}), (x_k,f_k)\\).  \nLet \\(h_1=x_{k-1}-x_{k-2}\\), \\(h_2=x_k-x_{k-1}\\),\n$$\n\\delta_1=\\frac{f_{k-1}-f_{k-2}}{h_1},\\quad\n\\delta_2=\\frac{f_k-f_{k-1}}{h_2}\n$$\n$$\nd=\\frac{\\delta_2-\\delta_1}{h_2\u002Bh_1},\\quad\nb=\\delta_2\u002Bh_2 d,\\quad\nD=\\sqrt{b^2-4 f_k d}\n$$\nChoose denominator with larger magnitude:\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=x_k-\\frac{2f_k}{b\\pm D}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef muller(f, x0, x1, x2, max_iter=100, tol=1e-12):\n    x0, x1, x2 = float(x0), float(x1), float(x2)\n    f0, f1, f2 = f(x0), f(x1), f(x2)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        h1, h2 = x1 - x0, x2 - x1\n        d1 = (f1 - f0) / h1\n        d2 = (f2 - f1) / h2\n        d = (d2 - d1) / (h1 \u002B h2)\n        b = d2 \u002B h2 * d\n        D = np.sqrt(b*b - 4.0*f2*d \u002B 0j)  # allow complex\n        denom = b \u002B D if abs(b \u002B D) \u003E abs(b - D) else b - D\n        if abs(denom) \u003C 1e-15:\n            raise ValueError(\u0022Denominator too small.\u0022)\n        dx = -2.0 * f2 / denom\n        x3 = x2 \u002B dx\n        if abs(dx) \u003C tol:\n            return x3\n        x0, x1, x2 = x1, x2, x3\n        f0, f1, f2 = f1, f2, f(x2)\n    return x2\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (first step)\n\\(f(x)=x^3-x-1\\), guesses \\(x_0=1\\), \\(x_1=1.5\\), \\(x_2=1.2\\).  \n\\(f_0=-1\\), \\(f_1=0.875\\), \\(f_2=-0.472\\).  \n\\(h_1=0.5\\), \\(h_2=-0.3\\).  \n\\(\\delta_1=(0.875-(-1))/0.5=3.75\\).  \n\\(\\delta_2=(-0.472-0.875)/(-0.3)=4.49\\).  \n\\(d=(4.49-3.75)/(0.2)=3.7\\).  \n\\(b=\\delta_2\u002Bh_2 d=4.49\u002B(-0.3)(3.7)=3.38\\).  \nThen compute \\(D\\) and update \\(x_3\\).\n\n---\n\n## 17) Brent\u0027s method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nBrent combines **bisection** (guaranteed bracketing) with **secant/inverse quadratic interpolation** (fast). Maintain bracket \\([a,b]\\) with \\(f(a)f(b)\u003C0\\); propose IQI/secant step if “safe,” otherwise bisection.\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef brent(f, a, b, max_iter=200, tol=1e-12):\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n    fa, fb = f(a), f(b)\n    if fa * fb \u003E 0:\n        raise ValueError(\u0022Root must be bracketed.\u0022)\n    c, fc = a, fa\n    d = e = b - a\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        if abs(fc) \u003C abs(fb):\n            a, b, c = b, c, b\n            fa, fb, fc = fb, fc, fb\n\n        tol1 = 2*np.finfo(float).eps*abs(b) \u002B 0.5*tol\n        m = 0.5*(c - b)\n        if abs(m) \u003C= tol1 or fb == 0:\n            return b\n\n        if abs(e) \u003E= tol1 and abs(fa) \u003E abs(fb):\n            s = fb / fa\n            if a == c:\n                p = 2*m*s\n                q = 1 - s\n            else:\n                q = fa / fc\n                r = fb / fc\n                p = s*(2*m*q*(q - r) - (b - a)*(r - 1))\n                q = (q - 1)*(r - 1)*(s - 1)\n            if p \u003E 0:\n                q = -q\n            p = abs(p)\n            if 2*p \u003C min(3*m*q - abs(tol1*q), abs(e*q)):\n                e, d = d, p / q\n            else:\n                e, d = d, m\n        else:\n            e, d = d, m\n\n        a, fa = b, fb\n        b = b \u002B (d if abs(d) \u003E tol1 else (tol1 if m \u003E 0 else -tol1))\n        fb = f(b)\n        if fb * fc \u003E 0:\n            c, fc = a, fa\n            d = e = b - a\n    return b\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (key intermediates)\nSame \\(f(x)=x^2-2\\), bracket \\([1,2]\\). Brent will:\n- keep bracket sign change,\n- attempt secant \\(x\\approx 1.3333\\),\n- fall back to bisection when interpolation step would leave bracket,\n- converge quickly to \\(1.41421356\\).\n\n---\n\n# Interpolation\n\n## 18) Lagrange interpolation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nGiven nodes \\((x_i,y_i)\\):\n$$\np(x)=\\sum_{i=0}^n y_i \\ell_i(x),\\quad\n\\ell_i(x)=\\prod_{j\\ne i}\\frac{x-x_j}{x_i-x_j}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef lagrange_interpolate(x_nodes, y_nodes, x):\n    x_nodes = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    y_nodes = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    x = float(x)\n    n = len(x_nodes)\n    p = 0.0\n    for i in range(n):\n        li = 1.0\n        for j in range(n):\n            if j != i:\n                li *= (x - x_nodes[j]) / (x_nodes[i] - x_nodes[j])\n        p \u002B= y_nodes[i] * li\n    return p\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nPoints \\((0,1),(1,3),(2,2)\\). Evaluate at \\(x=1.5\\).  \n\\(\\ell_0=(x-1)(x-2)/((0-1)(0-2))=(0.5)(-0.5)/(2)= -0.125\\).  \n\\(\\ell_1=(x-0)(x-2)/((1-0)(1-2))=(1.5)(-0.5)/(-1)=0.75\\).  \n\\(\\ell_2=(x-0)(x-1)/((2-0)(2-1))=(1.5)(0.5)/2=0.375\\).  \n\\(p(1.5)=1(-0.125)\u002B3(0.75)\u002B2(0.375)= -0.125\u002B2.25\u002B0.75=2.875\\).\n\n---\n\n## 19) Newton’s divided differences\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nPolynomial:\n$$\np(x)=c_0\u002Bc_1(x-x_0)\u002Bc_2(x-x_0)(x-x_1)\u002B\\cdots\n$$\nDivided differences:\n$$\nf[x_i]=y_i,\\quad\nf[x_i,\\dots,x_{i\u002Bk}]=\\frac{f[x_{i\u002B1},\\dots,x_{i\u002Bk}]-f[x_i,\\dots,x_{i\u002Bk-1}]}{x_{i\u002Bk}-x_i}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef newton_divided_differences(x_nodes, y_nodes):\n    x = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    coef = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1).copy()\n    n = len(x)\n    for j in range(1, n):\n        coef[j:n] = (coef[j:n] - coef[j-1:n-1]) / (x[j:n] - x[0:n-j])\n    return coef\n\ndef newton_eval(x_nodes, coef, x):\n    x_nodes = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    coef = _as_float_array(coef).reshape(-1)\n    x = float(x)\n    n = len(coef)\n    p = coef[-1]\n    for k in range(n - 2, -1, -1):\n        p = coef[k] \u002B (x - x_nodes[k]) * p\n    return p\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSame nodes \\(x=[0,1,2]\\), \\(y=[1,3,2]\\).  \nLevel1: \\(f[x0,x1]=(3-1)/(1-0)=2\\), \\(f[x1,x2]=(2-3)/(2-1)=-1\\).  \nLevel2: \\(f[x0,x1,x2]=(-1-2)/(2-0)=-1.5\\).  \nSo \\(p(x)=1\u002B2(x-0)-1.5(x-0)(x-1)\\).\n\n---\n\n## 20) Cubic spline interpolation (natural)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nPiecewise cubic \\(S_i(x)\\) with continuity of \\(S,S\u0027,S\u0027\u0027\\). Natural boundary: \\(S\u0027\u0027(x_0)=S\u0027\u0027(x_n)=0\\). Solve tridiagonal for second derivatives \\(M_i=S\u0027\u0027(x_i)\\):\nFor uniform notation \\(h_i=x_{i\u002B1}-x_i\\),\n$$\nh_{i-1}M_{i-1}\u002B2(h_{i-1}\u002Bh_i)M_i\u002Bh_iM_{i\u002B1}\n=6\\left(\\frac{y_{i\u002B1}-y_i}{h_i}-\\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef natural_cubic_spline(x_nodes, y_nodes):\n    x = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    y = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    n = len(x) - 1\n    h = x[1:] - x[:-1]\n\n    A = np.zeros((n\u002B1, n\u002B1))\n    rhs = np.zeros(n\u002B1)\n    A[0,0] = 1.0\n    A[n,n] = 1.0\n\n    for i in range(1, n):\n        A[i, i-1] = h[i-1]\n        A[i, i]   = 2*(h[i-1] \u002B h[i])\n        A[i, i\u002B1] = h[i]\n        rhs[i] = 6*((y[i\u002B1]-y[i])/h[i] - (y[i]-y[i-1])/h[i-1])\n\n    M = np.linalg.solve(A, rhs)\n\n    def S(xq):\n        xq = float(xq)\n        i = np.clip(np.searchsorted(x, xq) - 1, 0, n-1)\n        hi = h[i]\n        a = (x[i\u002B1] - xq)/hi\n        b = (xq - x[i])/hi\n        return (a*y[i] \u002B b*y[i\u002B1] \u002B\n                ((a**3 - a)*M[i] \u002B (b**3 - b)*M[i\u002B1])*(hi**2)/6.0)\n    return S, M\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (intermediate system)\nNodes \\((0,0),(1,1),(2,0)\\). \\(h_0=h_1=1\\). Natural: \\(M_0=M_2=0\\).  \nEquation for \\(i=1\\):\n\\(1\\cdot M_0 \u002B 2(1\u002B1)M_1 \u002B 1\\cdot M_2 = 6((0-1)/1 - (1-0)/1)=6(-1-1)=-12\\).  \nSo \\(4M_1=-12\\Rightarrow M_1=-3\\).  \nThen evaluate \\(S(0.5)\\) using the formula in code.\n\n---\n\n## 21) Hermite interpolation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nGiven \\(y_i=f(x_i)\\) and \\(y_i\u0027=f\u0027(x_i)\\). Hermite basis (for each node):\n$$\nH_i(x)=\\left(1-2L_i\u0027(x_i)(x-x_i)\\right)L_i(x)^2,\\quad\nK_i(x)=(x-x_i)L_i(x)^2\n$$\nHermite polynomial:\n$$\np(x)=\\sum_i \\bigl(y_i H_i(x) \u002B y_i\u0027 K_i(x)\\bigr)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef hermite_interpolate(x_nodes, y_nodes, dy_nodes, x):\n    x_nodes = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    y_nodes = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    dy_nodes = _as_float_array(dy_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    x = float(x)\n    n = len(x_nodes)\n\n    def L(i, xq):\n        val = 1.0\n        for j in range(n):\n            if j != i:\n                val *= (xq - x_nodes[j]) / (x_nodes[i] - x_nodes[j])\n        return val\n\n    def Lprime_at_i(i):\n        s = 0.0\n        for j in range(n):\n            if j != i:\n                s \u002B= 1.0 / (x_nodes[i] - x0=None, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-10):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    x = np.ones(n) if x0 is None else _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n    x = x / np.linalg.norm(x)\n\n    lam_old = 0.0\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        y = A @ x\n        x = y / np.linalg.norm(y)\n        lam = float(x.T @ (A @ x))\n        if abs(lam - lam_old) \u003C tol:\n            break\n        lam_old = lam\n    return lam, x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}2\u00261\\\\1\u00262\\end{bmatrix}\\), \\(x_0=(1,0)\\).  \n\\(y_1=Ax_0=(2,1)\\), \\(\\|y_1\\|=\\sqrt5\\), \\(x_1=(2/\\sqrt5,1/\\sqrt5)\\).  \nRayleigh: \\(\\lambda_1=x_1^TAx_1=3 - \\frac{2}{5}=2.6\\) (intermediate value).  \nNext iteration increases toward \\(3\\).\n\n---\n\n## 8) Jacobi iteration\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nSplit \\(A=D\u002BL\u002BU\\) (D diagonal). Jacobi:\n$$\nx^{(k\u002B1)} = D^{-1}\\bigl(b-(L\u002BU)x^{(k)}\\bigr)\n$$\nComponent form:\n$$\nx_i^{(k\u002B1)}=\\frac{1}{a_{ii}}\\left(b_i-\\sum_{j\\ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef jacobi_iteration(A, b, x0=None, max_iter=500, tol=1e-10):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    x = np.zeros(n) if x0 is None else _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n\n    D = np.diag(A)\n    R = A - np.diagflat(D)\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        x_new = (b - R @ x) / D\n        if _norm_inf(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x = x_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSolve:\n\\(\\;10x\u002By=11,\\; x\u002B10y=11\\). Start \\(x^{(0)}=(0,0)\\).  \n\\(x_1^{(1)}=(11-0)/10=1.1\\), \\(y^{(1)}=(11-0)/10=1.1\\).  \nNext: \\(x^{(2)}=(11-1.1)/10=0.99\\), \\(y^{(2)}=(11-1.1)/10=0.99\\). Converges to \\((1,1)\\).\n\n---\n\n## 9) Gauss–Seidel method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nUse newest values immediately:\n$$\nx_i^{(k\u002B1)}=\\frac{1}{a_{ii}}\\left(b_i-\\sum_{j\u003Ci}a_{ij}x_j^{(k\u002B1)}-\\sum_{j\u003Ei}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef gauss_seidel(A, b, x0=None, max_iter=500, tol=1e-10):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    x = np.zeros(n) if x0 is None else _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        x_old = x.copy()\n        for i in range(n):\n            s1 = np.dot(A[i, :i], x[:i])\n            s2 = np.dot(A[i, i\u002B1:], x_old[i\u002B1:])\n            x[i] = (b[i] - s1 - s2) / A[i, i]\n        if _norm_inf(x - x_old) \u003C tol:\n            return x\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSame system \\(10x\u002By=11,\\;x\u002B10y=11\\), \\(x^{(0)}=(0,0)\\).  \nIter1: \\(x^{(1)}=(11-0)/10=1.1\\).  \nThen \\(y^{(1)}=(11-1.1)/10=0.99\\).  \nIter2: \\(x^{(2)}=(11-0.99)/10=1.001\\); \\(y^{(2)}=(11-1.001)/10=0.9999\\). Faster than Jacobi.\n\n---\n\n## 10) Conjugate gradient method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nSolve SPD \\(Ax=b\\) minimizing:\n$$\nf(x)=\\frac12 x^TAx-b^Tx,\\quad \\nabla f = Ax-b=-r\n$$\nIteration (common form):\n$$\nr_0=b-Ax_0,\\; p_0=r_0\n$$\n$$\n\\alpha_k=\\frac{r_k^Tr_k}{p_k^TAp_k},\\quad x_{k\u002B1}=x_k\u002B\\alpha_k p_k\n$$\n$$\nr_{k\u002B1}=r_k-\\alpha_kAp_k,\\quad\n\\beta_k=\\frac{r_{k\u002B1}^Tr_{k\u002B1}}{r_k^Tr_k},\\quad\np_{k\u002B1}=r_{k\u002B1}\u002B\\beta_k p_k\n$$\n(See standard derivations and discussions in CG references.) [6][4][7]\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef conjugate_gradient(A, b, x0=None, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-10):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n    n = A.shape[0]\n    x = np.zeros(n) if x0 is None else _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n\n    r = b - A @ x\n    p = r.copy()\n    rs_old = float(r @ r)\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        Ap = A @ p\n        alpha = rs_old / float(p @ Ap)\n        x = x \u002B alpha * p\n        r = r - alpha * Ap\n        rs_new = float(r @ r)\n        if np.sqrt(rs_new) \u003C tol:\n            return x\n        beta = rs_new / rs_old\n        p = r \u002B beta * p\n        rs_old = rs_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}4\u00261\\\\1\u00263\\end{bmatrix}\\), \\(b=(1,2)\\), \\(x_0=(0,0)\\).  \n\\(r_0=b=(1,2)\\), \\(p_0=r_0\\).  \n\\(Ap_0=(4*1\u002B1*2,\\;1*1\u002B3*2)=(6,7)\\).  \n\\(\\alpha_0=(r_0^Tr_0)/(p_0^TAp_0)=(1^2\u002B2^2)/(1*6\u002B2*7)=5/20=0.25\\).  \n\\(x_1=(0,0)\u002B0.25(1,2)=(0.25,0.5)\\).  \n\\(r_1=r_0-\\alpha_0Ap_0=(1,2)-0.25(6,7)=(1-1.5,\\;2-1.75)=(-0.5,0.25)\\).  \nContinue similarly; in exact arithmetic CG solves 2×2 in ≤2 steps.\n\n---\n\n## 11) Least squares fitting\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nGiven \\(A\\in\\mathbb{R}^{m\\times n}\\), minimize \\(\\|Ax-b\\|_2^2\\).  \nNormal equations:\n$$\nA^TAx=A^Tb\n$$\nQR approach (preferred numerically):\n$$\nA=QR,\\quad \\min \\|QRx-b\\| \\Rightarrow Rx=Q^Tb\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef least_squares_qr(A, b):\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n    Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A, mode=\u0022reduced\u0022)\n    y = Q.T @ b\n    x = np.linalg.solve(R, y)\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nFit line \\(y\\approx c_0\u002Bc_1x\\) to points \\((0,1),(1,2),(2,2)\\).  \n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}1\u00260\\\\1\u00261\\\\1\u00262\\end{bmatrix}\\), \\(b=(1,2,2)\\).  \nCompute \\(A^TA=\\begin{bmatrix}3\u00263\\\\3\u00265\\end{bmatrix}\\), \\(A^Tb=(5,6)\\).  \nSolve:\n\\(\\begin{bmatrix}3\u00263\\\\3\u00265\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}c_0\\\\c_1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}5\\\\6\\end{bmatrix}\\).  \nEliminate: row2-row1 ⇒ \\(2c_1=1\\Rightarrow c_1=0.5\\).  \nThen \\(3c_0\u002B3*0.5=5\\Rightarrow 3c_0=3.5\\Rightarrow c_0=1.1667\\).\n\n---\n\n# Root Finding\n\n## 12) Bisection method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nIf \\(f(a)f(b)\u003C0\\), root in \\([a,b]\\). Midpoint \\(c=(a\u002Bb)/2\\).  \nShrink interval based on sign:\n$$\n(a,b)\\leftarrow\n\\begin{cases}\n(a,c),\u0026 f(a)f(c)\u003C0\\\\\n(c,b),\u0026 f(c)f(b)\u003C0\n\\end{cases}\n$$\nError bound after \\(n\\) steps:\n$$\n|x^*-c_n|\\le \\frac{b-a}{2^{n\u002B1}}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef bisection(f, a, b, max_iter=200, tol=1e-12):\n    fa, fb = f(a), f(b)\n    if fa * fb \u003E 0:\n        raise ValueError(\u0022f(a) and f(b) must have opposite signs.\u0022)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        c = 0.5 * (a \u002B b)\n        fc = f(c)\n        if abs(fc) \u003C tol or 0.5 * (b - a) \u003C tol:\n            return c\n        if fa * fc \u003C 0:\n            b, fb = c, fc\n        else:\n            a, fa = c, fc\n    return 0.5 * (a \u002B b)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nFind root of \\(f(x)=x^2-2\\) on \\([1,2]\\).  \n\\(f(1)=-1\\), \\(f(2)=2\\).  \n1) \\(c=1.5\\), \\(f(c)=0.25\u003E0\\Rightarrow [1,1.5]\\)  \n2) \\(c=1.25\\), \\(f=-0.4375\u003C0\\Rightarrow [1.25,1.5]\\)  \n3) \\(c=1.375\\), \\(f=-0.109375\u003C0\\Rightarrow [1.375,1.5]\\)  \n4) \\(c=1.4375\\), \\(f=0.06640625\u003E0\\Rightarrow [1.375,1.4375]\\) … converges to \\(\\sqrt2\\).\n\n---\n\n## 13) Newton–Raphson\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nLinearize:\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=x_k-\\frac{f(x_k)}{f\u0027(x_k)}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef newton_raphson(f, df, x0, max_iter=100, tol=1e-12):\n    x = float(x0)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        fx = f(x)\n        dfx = df(x)\n        if abs(dfx) \u003C 1e-15:\n            raise ValueError(\u0022Derivative too small.\u0022)\n        x_new = x - fx / dfx\n        if abs(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x = x_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(f(x)=x^2-2\\), \\(f\u0027(x)=2x\\), start \\(x_0=1.5\\).  \n\\(x_1=1.5-\\frac{0.25}{3}=1.4166667\\).  \n\\(f(x_1)=1.4166667^2-2=0.0069444\\).  \n\\(x_2=1.4166667-\\frac{0.0069444}{2.8333334}=1.4142157\\).\n\n---\n\n## 14) Secant method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nApproximate derivative by secant slope:\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=x_k-f(x_k)\\frac{x_k-x_{k-1}}{f(x_k)-f(x_{k-1})}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef secant(f, x0, x1, max_iter=200, tol=1e-12):\n    x_prev, x = float(x0), float(x1)\n    f_prev, fx = f(x_prev), f(x)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        denom = fx - f_prev\n        if abs(denom) \u003C 1e-15:\n            raise ValueError(\u0022Zero secant slope.\u0022)\n        x_new = x - fx * (x - x_prev) / denom\n        if abs(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x_prev, f_prev = x, fx\n        x, fx = x_new, f(x_new)\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(f(x)=x^2-2\\), \\(x_0=1\\), \\(x_1=2\\).  \n\\(x_2=2-2\\cdot(2-1)/(2-(-1))=2-2/3=1.3333333\\).  \n\\(f(x_2)=-0.2222222\\).  \n\\(x_3=1.3333333-(-0.2222)(1.3333-2)/(-0.2222-2)=1.4\\).\n\n---\n\n## 15) Fixed-point iteration\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nRewrite \\(x=g(x)\\). Iterate:\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=g(x_k)\n$$\nConverges if \\(|g\u0027(x^*)|\u003C1\\) near fixed point.\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef fixed_point(g, x0, max_iter=500, tol=1e-12):\n    x = float(x0)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        x_new = float(g(x))\n        if abs(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x = x_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSolve \\(x=\\cos x\\). Take \\(g(x)=\\cos x\\), \\(x_0=1\\).  \n\\(x_1=\\cos1=0.5403023\\)  \n\\(x_2=\\cos0.5403023=0.8575532\\)  \n\\(x_3=\\cos0.8575532=0.6542898\\) … converges to ~0.739085.\n\n---\n\n## 16) Müller\u0027s method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nQuadratic through \\((x_{k-2},f_{k-2}), (x_{k-1},f_{k-1}), (x_k,f_k)\\).  \nLet \\(h_1=x_{k-1}-x_{k-2}\\), \\(h_2=x_k-x_{k-1}\\),\n$$\n\\delta_1=\\frac{f_{k-1}-f_{k-2}}{h_1},\\quad\n\\delta_2=\\frac{f_k-f_{k-1}}{h_2}\n$$\n$$\nd=\\frac{\\delta_2-\\delta_1}{h_2\u002Bh_1},\\quad\nb=\\delta_2\u002Bh_2 d,\\quad\nD=\\sqrt{b^2-4 f_k d}\n$$\nChoose denominator with larger magnitude:\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=x_k-\\frac{2f_k}{b\\pm D}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef muller(f, x0, x1, x2, max_iter=100, tol=1e-12):\n    x0, x1, x2 = float(x0), float(x1), float(x2)\n    f0, f1, f2 = f(x0), f(x1), f(x2)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        h1, h2 = x1 - x0, x2 - x1\n        d1 = (f1 - f0) / h1\n        d2 = (f2 - f1) / h2\n        d = (d2 - d1) / (h1 \u002B h2)\n        b = d2 \u002B h2 * d\n        D = np.sqrt(b*b - 4.0*f2*d \u002B 0j)  # allow complex\n        denom = b \u002B D if abs(b \u002B D) \u003E abs(b - D) else b - D\n        if abs(denom) \u003C 1e-15:\n            raise ValueError(\u0022Denominator too small.\u0022)\n        dx = -2.0 * f2 / denom\n        x3 = x2 \u002B dx\n        if abs(dx) \u003C tol:\n            return x3\n        x0, x1, x2 = x1, x2, x3\n        f0, f1, f2 = f1, f2, f(x2)\n    return x2\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (first step)\n\\(f(x)=x^3-x-1\\), guesses \\(x_0=1\\), \\(x_1=1.5\\), \\(x_2=1.2\\).  \n\\(f_0=-1\\), \\(f_1=0.875\\), \\(f_2=-0.472\\).  \n\\(h_1=0.5\\), \\(h_2=-0.3\\).  \n\\(\\delta_1=(0.875-(-1))/0.5=3.75\\).  \n\\(\\delta_2=(-0.472-0.875)/(-0.3)=4.49\\).  \n\\(d=(4.49-3.75)/(0.2)=3.7\\).  \n\\(b=\\delta_2\u002Bh_2 d=4.49\u002B(-0.3)(3.7)=3.38\\).  \nThen compute \\(D\\) and update \\(x_3\\).\n\n---\n\n## 17) Brent\u0027s method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nBrent combines **bisection** (guaranteed bracketing) with **secant/inverse quadratic interpolation** (fast). Maintain bracket \\([a,b]\\) with \\(f(a)f(b)\u003C0\\); propose IQI/secant step if “safe,” otherwise bisection.\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef brent(f, a, b, max_iter=200, tol=1e-12):\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n    fa, fb = f(a), f(b)\n    if fa * fb \u003E 0:\n        raise ValueError(\u0022Root must be bracketed.\u0022)\n    c, fc = a, fa\n    d = e = b - a\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        if abs(fc) \u003C abs(fb):\n            a, b, c = b, c, b\n            fa, fb, fc = fb, fc, fb\n\n        tol1 = 2*np.finfo(float).eps*abs(b) \u002B 0.5*tol\n        m = 0.5*(c - b)\n        if abs(m) \u003C= tol1 or fb == 0:\n            return b\n\n        if abs(e) \u003E= tol1 and abs(fa) \u003E abs(fb):\n            s = fb / fa\n            if a == c:\n                p = 2*m*s\n                q = 1 - s\n            else:\n                q = fa / fc\n                r = fb / fc\n                p = s*(2*m*q*(q - r) - (b - a)*(r - 1))\n                q = (q - 1)*(r - 1)*(s - 1)\n            if p \u003E 0:\n                q = -q\n            p = abs(p)\n            if 2*p \u003C min(3*m*q - abs(tol1*q), abs(e*q)):\n                e, d = d, p / q\n            else:\n                e, d = d, m\n        else:\n            e, d = d, m\n\n        a, fa = b, fb\n        b = b \u002B (d if abs(d) \u003E tol1 else (tol1 if m \u003E 0 else -tol1))\n        fb = f(b)\n        if fb * fc \u003E 0:\n            c, fc = a, fa\n            d = e = b - a\n    return b\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (key intermediates)\nSame \\(f(x)=x^2-2\\), bracket \\([1,2]\\). Brent will:\n- keep bracket sign change,\n- attempt secant \\(x\\approx 1.3333\\),\n- fall back to bisection when interpolation step would leave bracket,\n- converge quickly to \\(1.41421356\\).\n\n---\n\n# Interpolation\n\n## 18) Lagrange interpolation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nGiven nodes \\((x_i,y_i)\\):\n$$\np(x)=\\sum_{i=0}^n y_i \\ell_i(x),\\quad\n\\ell_i(x)=\\prod_{j\\ne i}\\frac{x-x_j}{x_i-x_j}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef lagrange_interpolate(x_nodes, y_nodes, x):\n    x_nodes = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    y_nodes = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    x = float(x)\n    n = len(x_nodes)\n    p = 0.0\n    for i in range(n):\n        li = 1.0\n        for j in range(n):\n            if j != i:\n                li *= (x - x_nodes[j]) / (x_nodes[i] - x_nodes[j])\n        p \u002B= y_nodes[i] * li\n    return p\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nPoints \\((0,1),(1,3),(2,2)\\). Evaluate at \\(x=1.5\\).  \n\\(\\ell_0=(x-1)(x-2)/((0-1)(0-2))=(0.5)(-0.5)/(2)= -0.125\\).  \n\\(\\ell_1=(x-0)(x-2)/((1-0)(1-2))=(1.5)(-0.5)/(-1)=0.75\\).  \n\\(\\ell_2=(x-0)(x-1)/((2-0)(2-1))=(1.5)(0.5)/2=0.375\\).  \n\\(p(1.5)=1(-0.125)\u002B3(0.75)\u002B2(0.375)= -0.125\u002B2.25\u002B0.75=2.875\\).\n\n---\n\n## 19) Newton’s divided differences\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nPolynomial:\n$$\np(x)=c_0\u002Bc_1(x-x_0)\u002Bc_2(x-x_0)(x-x_1)\u002B\\cdots\n$$\nDivided differences:\n$$\nf[x_i]=y_i,\\quad\nf[x_i,\\dots,x_{i\u002Bk}]=\\frac{f[x_{i\u002B1},\\dots,x_{i\u002Bk}]-f[x_i,\\dots,x_{i\u002Bk-1}]}{x_{i\u002Bk}-x_i}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef newton_divided_differences(x_nodes, y_nodes):\n    x = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    coef = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1).copy()\n    n = len(x)\n    for j in range(1, n):\n        coef[j:n] = (coef[j:n] - coef[j-1:n-1]) / (x[j:n] - x[0:n-j])\n    return coef\n\ndef newton_eval(x_nodes, coef, x):\n    x_nodes = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    coef = _as_float_array(coef).reshape(-1)\n    x = float(x)\n    n = len(coef)\n    p = coef[-1]\n    for k in range(n - 2, -1, -1):\n        p = coef[k] \u002B (x - x_nodes[k]) * p\n    return p\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSame nodes \\(x=[0,1,2]\\), \\(y=[1,3,2]\\).  \nLevel1: \\(f[x0,x1]=(3-1)/(1-0)=2\\), \\(f[x1,x2]=(2-3)/(2-1)=-1\\).  \nLevel2: \\(f[x0,x1,x2]=(-1-2)/(2-0)=-1.5\\).  \nSo \\(p(x)=1\u002B2(x-0)-1.5(x-0)(x-1)\\).\n\n---\n\n## 20) Cubic spline interpolation (natural)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nPiecewise cubic \\(S_i(x)\\) with continuity of \\(S,S\u0027,S\u0027\u0027\\). Natural boundary: \\(S\u0027\u0027(x_0)=S\u0027\u0027(x_n)=0\\). Solve tridiagonal for second derivatives \\(M_i=S\u0027\u0027(x_i)\\):\nFor uniform notation \\(h_i=x_{i\u002B1}-x_i\\),\n$$\nh_{i-1}M_{i-1}\u002B2(h_{i-1}\u002Bh_i)M_i\u002Bh_iM_{i\u002B1}\n=6\\left(\\frac{y_{i\u002B1}-y_i}{h_i}-\\frac{y_i-y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef natural_cubic_spline(x_nodes, y_nodes):\n    x = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    y = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    n = len(x) - 1\n    h = x[1:] - x[:-1]\n\n    A = np.zeros((n\u002B1, n\u002B1))\n    rhs = np.zeros(n\u002B1)\n    A[0,0] = 1.0\n    A[n,n] = 1.0\n\n    for i in range(1, n):\n        A[i, i-1] = h[i-1]\n        A[i, i]   = 2*(h[i-1] \u002B h[i])\n        A[i, i\u002B1] = h[i]\n        rhs[i] = 6*((y[i\u002B1]-y[i])/h[i] - (y[i]-y[i-1])/h[i-1])\n\n    M = np.linalg.solve(A, rhs)\n\n    def S(xq):\n        xq = float(xq)\n        i = np.clip(np.searchsorted(x, xq) - 1, 0, n-1)\n        hi = h[i]\n        a = (x[i\u002B1] - xq)/hi\n        b = (xq - x[i])/hi\n        return (a*y[i] \u002B b*y[i\u002B1] \u002B\n                ((a**3 - a)*M[i] \u002B (b**3 - b)*M[i\u002B1])*(hi**2)/6.0)\n    return S, M\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (intermediate system)\nNodes \\((0,0),(1,1),(2,0)\\). \\(h_0=h_1=1\\). Natural: \\(M_0=M_2=0\\).  \nEquation for \\(i=1\\):\n\\(1\\cdot M_0 \u002B 2(1\u002B1)M_1 \u002B 1\\cdot M_2 = 6((0-1)/1 - (1-0)/1)=6(-1-1)=-12\\).  \nSo \\(4M_1=-12\\Rightarrow M_1=-3\\).  \nThen evaluate \\(S(0.5)\\) using the formula in code.\n\n---\n\n## 21) Hermite interpolation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nGiven \\(y_i=f(x_i)\\) and \\(y_i\u0027=f\u0027(x_i)\\). Hermite basis (for each node):\n$$\nH_i(x)=\\left(1-2L_i\u0027(x_i)(x-x_i)\\right)L_i(x)^2,\\quad\nK_i(x)=(x-x_i)L_i(x)^2\n$$\nHermite polynomial:\n$$\np(x)=\\sum_i \\bigl(y_i H_i(x) \u002B y_i\u0027 K_i(x)\\bigr)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef hermite_interpolate(x_nodes, y_nodes, dy_nodes, x):\n    x_nodes = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    y_nodes = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    dy_nodes = _as_float_array(dy_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    x = float(x)\n    n = len(x_nodes)\n\n    def L(i, xq):\n        val = 1.0\n        for j in range(n):\n            if j != i:\n                val *= (xq - x_nodes[j]) / (x_nodes[i] - x_nodes[j])\n        return val\n\n    def Lprime_at_i(i):\n        s = 0.0\n        for j in range(n):\n            if j != i:\n                s \u002B= 1.0 / (x_nodes[i] - x_nodes[j])\n        return s\n\n    p = 0.0\n    for i in range(n):\n        Li = L(i, x)\n        Lpi = Lprime_at_i(i)\n        Hi = (1 - 2*Lpi*(x - x_nodes[i])) * (Li**2)\n        Ki = (x - x_nodes[i]) * (Li**2)\n        p \u002B= y_nodes[i]*Hi \u002B dy_nodes[i]*Ki\n    return p\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nInterpolate \\(f\\) with \\(f(0)=1,f\u0027(0)=0\\); \\(f(1)=2,f\u0027(1)=1\\).  \nCompute at \\(x=0.5\\).  \nFor 2 nodes, \\(L_0(x)=1-x\\), \\(L_1(x)=x\\).  \n\\(L_0\u0027(0)=-1\\), \\(L_1\u0027(1)=1\\).  \nThen \\(H_0=(1-2(-1)(x-0))(1-x)^2=(1\u002B2x)(1-x)^2\\), \\(K_0=x(1-x)^2\\).  \n\\(H_1=(1-2(1)(x-1))x^2=(3-2x)x^2\\), \\(K_1=(x-1)x^2\\).  \nPlug \\(x=0.5\\) to get numeric intermediate values.\n\n---\n\n## 22) Chebyshev interpolation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nChebyshev nodes on \\([-1,1]\\):\n$$\nx_k=\\cos\\left(\\frac{(2k\u002B1)\\pi}{2(n\u002B1)}\\right),\\;k=0,\\dots,n\n$$\nInterpolate using barycentric formula:\n$$\np(x)=\\frac{\\sum_{k=0}^n \\frac{w_k}{x-x_k} y_k}{\\sum_{k=0}^n \\frac{w_k}{x-x_k}}\n$$\nChebyshev barycentric weights (first kind): \\(w_k=(-1)^k\\).\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef chebyshev_nodes(n):\n    k = np.arange(n\u002B1)\n    return np.cos((2*k \u002B 1) * np.pi / (2*(n\u002B1)))\n\ndef barycentric_interpolate(x_nodes, y_nodes, x, weights=None):\n    x_nodes = _as_float_array(x_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    y_nodes = _as_float_array(y_nodes).reshape(-1)\n    x = float(x)\n    n = len(x_nodes)\n    if weights is None:\n        weights = np.ones(n)\n    weights = _as_float_array(weights).reshape(-1)\n\n    dif = x - x_nodes\n    j = np.where(np.abs(dif) \u003C 1e-15)[0]\n    if len(j) \u003E 0:\n        return float(y_nodes[j[0]])\n\n    num = np.sum(weights * y_nodes / dif)\n    den = np.sum(weights / dif)\n    return float(num / den)\n\ndef chebyshev_interpolate(f, n, x):\n    xs = chebyshev_nodes(n)\n    ys = np.array([f(xi) for xi in xs], dtype=float)\n    ws = np.array([(-1.0)**k for k in range(n\u002B1)], dtype=float)\n    return barycentric_interpolate(xs, ys, x, ws)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nApproximate \\(f(x)=1/(1\u002B25x^2)\\) with \\(n=4\\).  \nCompute nodes:\n\\(x_0=\\cos(\\pi/10)\\approx0.9511\\), \\(x_1=\\cos(3\\pi/10)\\approx0.5878\\), …  \nCompute \\(y_k=f(x_k)\\).  \nEvaluate at \\(x=0\\): barycentric simplifies since \\(x-x_k=-x_k\\), show numerator/denominator sums explicitly.\n\n---\n\n# Numerical Integration\n\n## 23) Trapezoidal rule\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nSingle interval:\n$$\n\\int_a^b f(x)\\,dx \\approx \\frac{b-a}{2}\\left(f(a)\u002Bf(b)\\right)\n$$\nComposite with step \\(h=(b-a)/n\\):\n$$\n\\int_a^b f(x)\\,dx\\approx h\\left(\\frac12 f(a)\u002B\\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}f(a\u002Bih)\u002B\\frac12 f(b)\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef trapezoidal(f, a, b, n=1):\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n    n = int(n)\n    h = (b - a) / n\n    s = 0.5 * (f(a) \u002B f(b))\n    for i in range(1, n):\n        s \u002B= f(a \u002B i*h)\n    return h * s\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nIntegrate \\(f(x)=x^2\\) on \\([0,1]\\) with \\(n=2\\). \\(h=0.5\\).  \nValues: \\(f(0)=0\\), \\(f(0.5)=0.25\\), \\(f(1)=1\\).  \nComposite trap:\n\\(I\\approx 0.5[0.5*0 \u002B 0.25 \u002B 0.5*1]=0.5[0.25\u002B0.5]=0.375\\). Exact \\(=1/3\\approx0.3333\\).\n\n---\n\n## 24) Simpson’s 1/3 rule\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFor even \\(n\\), step \\(h\\):\n$$\n\\int_a^b f(x)\\,dx\\approx \\frac{h}{3}\\left[f(x_0)\u002B4\\sum_{i\\ \\text{odd}}f(x_i)\u002B2\\sum_{i\\ \\text{even},\\,i\\ne 0,n}f(x_i)\u002Bf(x_n)\\right]\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef simpson_1_3(f, a, b, n=2):\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n    n = int(n)\n    if n % 2 != 0:\n        raise ValueError(\u0022n must be even.\u0022)\n    h = (b - a) / n\n    s = f(a) \u002B f(b)\n    for i in range(1, n):\n        s \u002B= (4 if i % 2 == 1 else 2) * f(a \u002B i*h)\n    return (h/3.0) * s\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(f(x)=x^2\\), \\([0,1]\\), \\(n=2\\), \\(h=0.5\\).  \n\\(I\\approx (0.5/3)[f(0)\u002B4f(0.5)\u002Bf(1)]=(1/6)[0\u002B4*0.25\u002B1]=(1/6)*2=0.333333\\) exact.\n\n---\n\n## 25) Simpson’s 3/8 rule\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFor \\(n\\) multiple of 3, step \\(h\\):\n$$\n\\int_a^b f(x)\\,dx\\approx \\frac{3h}{8}\\left[f_0\u002B3(f_1\u002Bf_2)\u002B2(f_3\u002Bf_6\u002B\\cdots)\u002B3(\\cdots)\u002Bf_n\\right]\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef simpson_3_8(f, a, b, n=3):\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n    n = int(n)\n    if n % 3 != 0:\n        raise ValueError(\u0022n must be multiple of 3.\u0022)\n    h = (b - a) / n\n    s = f(a) \u002B f(b)\n    for i in range(1, n):\n        coef = 2 if i % 3 == 0 else 3\n        s \u002B= coef * f(a \u002B i*h)\n    return (3*h/8.0) * s\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(f(x)=x^3\\) on \\([0,1]\\), \\(n=3\\), \\(h=1/3\\).  \nValues: \\(f(0)=0\\), \\(f(1/3)=1/27\\), \\(f(2/3)=8/27\\), \\(f(1)=1\\).  \n\\(I\\approx (3h/8)[0\u002B3(1/27\u002B8/27)\u002B1]=(1/8)[3*(9/27)\u002B1]=(1/8)[1\u002B1]=0.25\\). Exact \\(\\int_0^1x^3dx=1/4\\).\n\n---\n\n## 26) Romberg integration\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nRichardson extrapolation on trapezoids:\n$$\nR_{0,0}=T(h),\\quad R_{k,0}=T(h/2^k)\n$$\n$$\nR_{k,j}=R_{k,j-1}\u002B\\frac{R_{k,j-1}-R_{k-1,j-1}}{4^j-1}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef romberg(f, a, b, levels=5):\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n    R = np.zeros((levels, levels))\n    R[0, 0] = trapezoidal(f, a, b, n=1)\n    for k in range(1, levels):\n        R[k, 0] = trapezoidal(f, a, b, n=2**k)\n        for j in range(1, k\u002B1):\n            R[k, j] = R[k, j-1] \u002B (R[k, j-1] - R[k-1, j-1]) / (4**j - 1)\n    return R\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(f(x)=\\sin x\\) on \\([0,\\pi]\\).  \n\\(R_{0,0}=T(n=1)=\\pi/2(\\sin0\u002B\\sin\\pi)=0\\).  \n\\(R_{1,0}=T(n=2)=\\frac{\\pi}{2}(\\tfrac12*0\u002B1\u002B\\tfrac12*0)=\\pi/2\\).  \n\\(R_{1,1}=R_{1,0}\u002B\\frac{R_{1,0}-R_{0,0}}{3}=\\pi/2\u002B\\pi/6=2\\pi/3\\approx2.094\\).  \nExact is \\(2\\).\n\n---\n\n## 27) Gaussian quadrature (Gauss–Legendre)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFor \\([-1,1]\\):\n$$\n\\int_{-1}^1 f(x)\\,dx \\approx \\sum_{i=1}^n w_i f(x_i)\n$$\nNodes \\(x_i\\) are roots of \\(P_n(x)\\), weights:\n$$\nw_i=\\frac{2}{(1-x_i^2)[P_n\u0027(x_i)]^2}\n$$\nMap \\([a,b]\\) via \\(x=\\frac{b-a}{2}t\u002B\\frac{a\u002Bb}{2}\\).\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef gauss_legendre(f, a, b, n=2):\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n    # Use numpy\u0027s built-in nodes/weights for Legendre\n    t, w = np.polynomial.legendre.leggauss(int(n))\n    xm = 0.5*(b \u002B a)\n    xr = 0.5*(b - a)\n    return xr * np.sum(w * np.array([f(xm \u002B xr*ti) for ti in t]))\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (n=2)\nNodes \\(t=\\pm 1/\\sqrt3\\), weights \\(w_1=w_2=1\\).  \nIntegrate \\(f(x)=x^2\\) on \\([-1,1]\\):  \nApprox \\(=1\\cdot f(-1/\\sqrt3)\u002B1\\cdot f(1/\\sqrt3)=2\\cdot(1/3)=2/3\\).  \nExact \\(\\int_{-1}^1x^2dx=2/3\\).\n\n---\n\n## 28) Monte Carlo integration\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFor uniform \\(X_i\\sim U(a,b)\\):\n$$\n\\int_a^b f(x)\\,dx \\approx (b-a)\\frac{1}{N}\\sum_{i=1}^N f(X_i)\n$$\nVariance \\(\\propto 1/N\\).\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef monte_carlo_integral(f, a, b, N=10000, seed=0):\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n    xs = rng.uniform(a, b, int(N))\n    return (b - a) * float(np.mean([f(x) for x in xs]))\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nEstimate \\(\\int_0^1 x^2 dx\\). Use samples \\(x=[0.2,0.5,0.9]\\) (toy \\(N=3\\)).  \nMean \\(f=\\frac{0.04\u002B0.25\u002B0.81}{3}=0.3666667\\).  \nEstimate \\(=1*0.3666667\\) (rough, improves as \\(N\\) increases).\n\n---\n\n## 29) Adaptive quadrature (adaptive Simpson)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nSimpson on \\([a,b]\\):\n$$\nS(a,b)=\\frac{b-a}{6}\\left(f(a)\u002B4f\\!\\left(\\frac{a\u002Bb}{2}\\right)\u002Bf(b)\\right)\n$$\nRecursively split until:\n$$\n|S(a,m)\u002BS(m,b)-S(a,b)| \u003C 15\\varepsilon\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef adaptive_simpson(f, a, b, eps=1e-10, max_depth=20):\n    a, b = float(a), float(b)\n\n    def S(a, b):\n        m = 0.5*(a\u002Bb)\n        return (b-a)/6.0 * (f(a) \u002B 4*f(m) \u002B f(b))\n\n    def rec(a, b, eps, whole, depth):\n        m = 0.5*(a\u002Bb)\n        left = S(a, m)\n        right = S(m, b)\n        if depth \u003C= 0 or abs(left \u002B right - whole) \u003C 15*eps:\n            return left \u002B right \u002B (left \u002B right - whole)/15.0\n        return rec(a, m, eps/2, left, depth-1) \u002B rec(m, b, eps/2, right, depth-1)\n\n    whole = S(a, b)\n    return rec(a, b, eps, whole, max_depth)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (first split)\nIntegrate \\(f(x)=\\sin x\\) on \\([0,\\pi]\\).  \nWhole Simpson: \\(S(0,\\pi)=\\pi/6(0\u002B4\\cdot1\u002B0)=2\\pi/3\\approx2.094\\).  \nSplit at \\(m=\\pi/2\\): compute \\(S(0,\\pi/2)\\) and \\(S(\\pi/2,\\pi)\\), compare and refine until tolerance.\n\n---\n\n# ODEs\n\n## 30) Euler’s method\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFor \\(y\u0027=f(t,y)\\), step \\(h\\):\n$$\ny_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002Bh f(t_n,y_n)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef euler(f, t0, y0, h, n_steps):\n    t = float(t0)\n    y = float(y0)\n    out = [(t, y)]\n    for _ in range(int(n_steps)):\n        y = y \u002B h * f(t, y)\n        t = t \u002B h\n        out.append((t, y))\n    return out\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(y\u0027=y\\), \\(y(0)=1\\), \\(h=0.5\\).  \nStep1: \\(y_1=1\u002B0.5*1=1.5\\).  \nStep2: \\(y_2=1.5\u002B0.5*1.5=2.25\\). Exact at \\(t=1\\) is \\(e\\approx2.718\\).\n\n---\n\n## 31) Heun’s method (improved Euler)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nPredictor \\(y^*=y_n\u002Bh f(t_n,y_n)\\). Corrector:\n$$\ny_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002B\\frac{h}{2}\\left[f(t_n,y_n)\u002Bf(t_{n\u002B1},y^*)\\right]\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef heun(f, t0, y0, h, n_steps):\n    t = float(t0)\n    y = float(y0)\n    out = [(t, y)]\n    for _ in range(int(n_steps)):\n        k1 = f(t, y)\n        y_pred = y \u002B h * k1\n        k2 = f(t \u002B h, y_pred)\n        y = y \u002B (h/2.0) * (k1 \u002B k2)\n        t = t \u002B h\n        out.append((t, y))\n    return out\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(y\u0027=y\\), \\(y(0)=1\\), \\(h=0.5\\).  \n\\(k1=1\\), \\(y^*=1.5\\), \\(k2=1.5\\).  \n\\(y_1=1\u002B0.25(1\u002B1.5)=1.625\\) (closer to \\(e^{0.5}=1.6487\\)).\n\n---\n\n## 32) Classical Runge–Kutta (RK4)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\n$$\nk_1=f(t_n,y_n)\n$$\n$$\nk_2=f\\left(t_n\u002B\\frac{h}{2},y_n\u002B\\frac{h}{2}k_1\\right),\\;\nk_3=f\\left(t_n\u002B\\frac{h}{2},y_n\u002B\\frac{h}{2}k_2\\right)\n$$\n$$\nk_4=f(t_n\u002Bh,y_n\u002Bhk_3)\n$$\n$$\ny_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002B\\frac{h}{6}(k_1\u002B2k_2\u002B2k_3\u002Bk_4)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef rk4(f, t0, y0, h, n_steps):\n    t = float(t0)\n    y = float(y0)\n    out = [(t, y)]\n    for _ in range(int(n_steps)):\n        k1 = f(t, y)\n        k2 = f(t \u002B h/2, y \u002B h*k1/2)\n        k3 = f(t \u002B h/2, y \u002B h*k2/2)\n        k4 = f(t \u002B h,   y \u002B h*k3)\n        y = y \u002B (h/6.0)*(k1 \u002B 2*k2 \u002B 2*k3 \u002B k4)\n        t = t \u002B h\n        out.append((t, y))\n    return out\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (one step)\n\\(y\u0027=y\\), \\(y(0)=1\\), \\(h=0.5\\).  \n\\(k1=1\\).  \n\\(k2=f(0.25,1.25)=1.25\\).  \n\\(k3=f(0.25,1.3125)=1.3125\\).  \n\\(k4=f(0.5,1.65625)=1.65625\\).  \n\\(y_1=1\u002B0.5/6(1\u002B2*1.25\u002B2*1.3125\u002B1.65625)=1.6484375\\) (very close to 1.64872).\n\n---\n\n## 33) Adaptive RK45 (Dormand–Prince)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nCompute 4th and 5th order estimates \\(y^{(4)},y^{(5)}\\); error \\(e=\\|y^{(5)}-y^{(4)}\\|\\). Update step:\n$$\nh_{\\text{new}} = h\\cdot \\left(\\frac{\\text{tol}}{e}\\right)^{1/5}\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef rk45_step(f, t, y, h):\n    # Dormand–Prince coefficients\n    k1 = f(t, y)\n    k2 = f(t \u002B h*(1/5), y \u002B h*(1/5)*k1)\n    k3 = f(t \u002B h*(3/10), y \u002B h*(3/40*k1 \u002B 9/40*k2))\n    k4 = f(t \u002B h*(4/5), y \u002B h*(44/45*k1 - 56/15*k2 \u002B 32/9*k3))\n    k5 = f(t \u002B h*(8/9), y \u002B h*(19372/6561*k1 - 25360/2187*k2 \u002B 64448/6561*k3 - 212/729*k4))\n    k6 = f(t \u002B h,       y \u002B h*(9017/3168*k1 - 355/33*k2 \u002B 46732/5247*k3 \u002B 49/176*k4 - 5103/18656*k5))\n    # 5th order\n    y5 = y \u002B h*(35/384*k1 \u002B 500/1113*k3 \u002B 125/192*k4 - 2187/6784*k5 \u002B 11/84*k6)\n    # 4th order (embedded)\n    k7 = f(t \u002B h, y5)\n    y4 = y \u002B h*(5179/57600*k1 \u002B 7571/16695*k3 \u002B 393/640*k4 - 92097/339200*k5 \u002B 187/2100*k6 \u002B 1/40*k7)\n    return y4, y5\n\ndef adaptive_rk45(f, t0, y0, t1, h0=0.1, tol=1e-8):\n    t = float(t0)\n    y = float(y0)\n    h = float(h0)\n    out = [(t, y)]\n    while t \u003C t1 - 1e-15:\n        if t \u002B h \u003E t1:\n            h = t1 - t\n        y4, y5 = rk45_step(f, t, y, h)\n        err = abs(y5 - y4)\n        if err \u003C tol or h \u003C 1e-15:\n            t = t \u002B h\n            y = float(y5)\n            out.append((t, y))\n        scale = (tol / max(err, 1e-15))**0.2\n        h = h * min(5.0, max(0.2, 0.9*scale))\n    return out\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (conceptual intermediates)\nFor \\(y\u0027=y\\), \\(y(0)=1\\), start \\(h=0.5\\).  \nCompute \\(y^{(4)}, y^{(5)}\\); suppose \\(err=|y5-y4|=2\\times10^{-7}\\) and tol \\(=10^{-8}\\).  \nScale factor \\((10^{-8}/2\\cdot10^{-7})^{1/5}=(0.05)^{0.2}\\approx0.549\\).  \nNew \\(h\\approx 0.9*0.549*0.5\\approx0.247\\).\n\n---\n\n## 34) Adams–Bashforth methods\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nExplicit multistep. AB2:\n$$\ny_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002B\\frac{h}{2}\\left(3f_n-f_{n-1}\\right)\n$$\nAB4:\n$$\ny_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002B\\frac{h}{24}\\left(55f_n-59f_{n-1}\u002B37f_{n-2}-9f_{n-3}\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation (AB2)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef adams_bashforth_2(f, t0, y0, h, n_steps):\n    # bootstrap one step with RK4 for y1\n    sol = rk4(f, t0, y0, h, 1)\n    (t0, y0), (t1, y1) = sol[0], sol[1]\n    out = [(t0, y0), (t1, y1)]\n    f0 = f(t0, y0)\n    f1 = f(t1, y1)\n    t, y = t1, y1\n    for _ in range(1, int(n_steps)):\n        y_next = y \u002B (h/2.0)*(3*f1 - f0)\n        t_next = t \u002B h\n        f0, f1 = f1, f(t_next, y_next)\n        t, y = t_next, y_next\n        out.append((t, y))\n    return out\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(y\u0027=y\\), \\(h=0.5\\).  \nBootstrap \\(y_1\\approx 1.6484375\\) (RK4).  \nThen \\(f_0=1\\), \\(f_1=1.6484375\\).  \nAB2: \\(y_2=y_1\u002B0.25(3*1.6484375-1)=1.6484375\u002B0.25(3.9453125)=2.6347656\\) (exact at \\(t=1\\) is 2.71828).\n\n---\n\n## 35) Backward Euler\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nImplicit:\n$$\ny_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002Bh f(t_{n\u002B1},y_{n\u002B1})\n$$\nSolve nonlinear equation each step (e.g., Newton).\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef backward_euler(f, dfdy, t0, y0, h, n_steps, newton_iters=20):\n    t = float(t0)\n    y = float(y0)\n    out = [(t, y)]\n    for _ in range(int(n_steps)):\n        t1 = t \u002B h\n        y_guess = y\n        for _it in range(newton_iters):\n            g = y_guess - y - h*f(t1, y_guess)\n            dg = 1.0 - h*dfdy(t1, y_guess)\n            y_new = y_guess - g/dg\n            if abs(y_new - y_guess) \u003C 1e-12:\n                y_guess = y_new\n                break\n            y_guess = y_new\n        y = float(y_guess)\n        t = t1\n        out.append((t, y))\n    return out\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(y\u0027=y\\). Backward Euler: \\(y_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002Bh y_{n\u002B1}\\Rightarrow y_{n\u002B1}=y_n/(1-h)\\).  \nWith \\(h=0.5\\), \\(y_1=1/(0.5)=2\\), \\(y_2=2/0.5=4\\) (stable for stiff decay problems, but grows here).\n\n---\n\n## 36) Crank–Nicolson\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nTrapezoid in time:\n$$\ny_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002B\\frac{h}{2}\\left(f(t_n,y_n)\u002Bf(t_{n\u002B1},y_{n\u002B1})\\right)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef crank_nicolson(f, dfdy, t0, y0, h, n_steps, newton_iters=20):\n    t = float(t0)\n    y = float(y0)\n    out = [(t, y)]\n    for _ in range(int(n_steps)):\n        t1 = t \u002B h\n        y_guess = y\n        fn = f(t, y)\n        for _it in range(newton_iters):\n            g = y_guess - y - (h/2.0)*(fn \u002B f(t1, y_guess))\n            dg = 1.0 - (h/2.0)*dfdy(t1, y_guess)\n            y_new = y_guess - g/dg\n            if abs(y_new - y_guess) \u003C 1e-12:\n                y_guess = y_new\n                break\n            y_guess = y_new\n        y = float(y_guess)\n        t = t1\n        out.append((t, y))\n    return out\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nFor \\(y\u0027=y\\): \\(y_{n\u002B1}=y_n\u002B\\frac{h}{2}(y_n\u002By_{n\u002B1})\\Rightarrow y_{n\u002B1}=\\frac{1\u002Bh/2}{1-h/2}y_n\\).  \nWith \\(h=0.5\\): factor \\(=(1.25)/(0.75)=1.6666667\\). So \\(y_1=1.6667\\).\n\n---\n\n# Optimization\n\n## 37) Gradient descent\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nMinimize \\(f(x)\\):\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=x_k-\\alpha_k\\nabla f(x_k)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef gradient_descent(grad, x0, alpha=0.1, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-10):\n    x = _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        g = _as_float_array(grad(x)).reshape(-1)\n        x_new = x - alpha * g\n        if np.linalg.norm(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x = x_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nMinimize \\(f(x)=(x-3)^2\\), \\(\\nabla f=2(x-3)\\), \\(x_0=0\\), \\(\\alpha=0.1\\).  \n\\(x_1=0-0.1*2(-3)=0.6\\).  \n\\(x_2=0.6-0.1*2(-2.4)=1.08\\). Converges to 3.\n\n---\n\n## 38) Newton’s method for optimization\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nUsing Hessian \\(H\\):\n$$\nx_{k\u002B1}=x_k-H(x_k)^{-1}\\nabla f(x_k)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef newton_opt(grad, hess, x0, max_iter=50, tol=1e-12):\n    x = _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        g = _as_float_array(grad(x)).reshape(-1)\n        H = _as_float_array(hess(x))\n        dx = np.linalg.solve(H, g)\n        x_new = x - dx\n        if np.linalg.norm(dx) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x = x_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSame \\(f(x)=(x-3)^2\\). \\(g=2(x-3)\\), \\(H=2\\).  \nFrom \\(x_0=0\\): \\(dx=g/H= -3\\). \\(x_1=0-(-3)=3\\) (one step).\n\n---\n\n## 39) BFGS\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nUpdate inverse Hessian approximation \\(B_k\\):\n$$\ns_k=x_{k\u002B1}-x_k,\\quad y_k=\\nabla f_{k\u002B1}-\\nabla f_k\n$$\n$$\nB_{k\u002B1}=(I-\\rho s y^T)B_k(I-\\rho y s^T)\u002B\\rho s s^T,\\quad \\rho=\\frac{1}{y^Ts}\n$$\n(Standard in optimization texts.) [3][8]\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef bfgs(grad, x0, alpha=0.1, max_iter=200, tol=1e-10):\n    x = _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n    n = len(x)\n    B = np.eye(n)\n    g = _as_float_array(grad(x)).reshape(-1)\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        p = -B @ g\n        x_new = x \u002B alpha * p\n        g_new = _as_float_array(grad(x_new)).reshape(-1)\n\n        s = (x_new - x).reshape(-1, 1)\n        y = (g_new - g).reshape(-1, 1)\n        ys = float(y.T @ s)\n        if abs(ys) \u003C 1e-15:\n            return x_new\n        rho = 1.0 / ys\n        I = np.eye(n)\n        B = (I - rho*s@y.T) @ B @ (I - rho*y@s.T) \u002B rho*(s@s.T)\n\n        if np.linalg.norm(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x, g = x_new, g_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (first update)\nMinimize \\(f(x)= (x-3)^2\\) in 1D. \\(B_0=1\\).  \n\\(g_0=2(x_0-3)\\). With \\(x_0=0\\), \\(g_0=-6\\), \\(p=6\\).  \nTake \\(\\alpha=0.1\\): \\(x_1=0.6\\). \\(g_1=2(-2.4)=-4.8\\).  \n\\(s=0.6\\), \\(y=1.2\\), \\(\\rho=1/(0.72)=1.3889\\). Update \\(B\\) accordingly.\n\n---\n\n## 40) L-BFGS\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nStore last \\(m\\) pairs \\((s_i,y_i)\\). Two-loop recursion gives \\(H_k g_k\\) without storing full matrices.\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef lbfgs(grad, x0, m=5, alpha=0.5, max_iter=200, tol=1e-10):\n    x = _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n    s_list, y_list, rho_list = [], [], []\n    g = _as_float_array(grad(x)).reshape(-1)\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        q = g.copy()\n        a = []\n        for s, y, rho in reversed(list(zip(s_list, y_list, rho_list))):\n            ai = rho * np.dot(s, q)\n            a.append(ai)\n            q = q - ai * y\n        # initial H0 scaling\n        if len(s_list) \u003E 0:\n            s, y = s_list[-1], y_list[-1]\n            gamma = np.dot(s, y) / max(np.dot(y, y), 1e-15)\n        else:\n            gamma = 1.0\n        r = gamma * q\n        for (s, y, rho), ai in zip(zip(s_list, y_list, rho_list), reversed(a)):\n            beta = rho * np.dot(y, r)\n            r = r \u002B s * (ai - beta)\n\n        p = -r\n        x_new = x \u002B alpha * p\n        g_new = _as_float_array(grad(x_new)).reshape(-1)\n\n        s = x_new - x\n        y = g_new - g\n        ys = np.dot(y, s)\n        if abs(ys) \u003E 1e-15:\n            rho = 1.0 / ys\n            s_list.append(s); y_list.append(y); rho_list.append(rho)\n            if len(s_list) \u003E m:\n                s_list.pop(0); y_list.pop(0); rho_list.pop(0)\n\n        if np.linalg.norm(x_new - x) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new\n        x, g = x_new, g_new\n    return x\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nSame 1D example: stores scalars \\(s,y\\) and produces quasi-Newton direction close to Newton step as iterations proceed.\n\n---\n\n## 41) Simplex method (LP)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nStandard form:\n$$\n\\max c^Tx\\quad\\text{s.t.}\\quad Ax\\le b,\\ x\\ge 0\n$$\nIntroduce slack \\(s\\ge0\\): \\(Ax\u002Bs=b\\). Pivot to improve objective until no negative reduced costs.\n\n### Python implementation (small, pedagogical)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef simplex_max(c, A, b, max_iter=100):\n    c = _as_float_array(c).reshape(-1)\n    A = _as_float_array(A)\n    b = _as_float_array(b).reshape(-1)\n\n    m, n = A.shape\n    T = np.zeros((m\u002B1, n\u002Bm\u002B1))\n    T[:m, :n] = A\n    T[:m, n:n\u002Bm] = np.eye(m)\n    T[:m, -1] = b\n    T[m, :n] = -c  # maximize\n\n    basis = list(range(n, n\u002Bm))\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        # entering: most negative in objective row\n        j = int(np.argmin(T[m, :-1]))\n        if T[m, j] \u003E= -1e-12:\n            break\n        col = T[:m, j]\n        if np.all(col \u003C= 1e-15):\n            raise ValueError(\u0022Unbounded.\u0022)\n        ratios = np.array([T[i, -1]/col[i] if col[i] \u003E 1e-15 else np.inf for i in range(m)])\n        i = int(np.argmin(ratios))\n        piv = T[i, j]\n        T[i, :] = T[i, :] / piv\n        for r in range(m\u002B1):\n            if r != i:\n                T[r, :] = T[r, :] - T[r, j] * T[i, :]\n        basis[i] = j\n\n    x = np.zeros(n\u002Bm)\n    for i, bi in enumerate(basis):\n        x[bi] = T[i, -1]\n    return x[:n], T[m, -1]\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nMaximize \\(z=3x\u002B2y\\) s.t. \\(x\u002By\\le4\\), \\(x\\le2\\), \\(y\\le3\\), \\(x,y\\ge0\\).  \nAt optimum: \\(x=2,y=2\\Rightarrow z=10\\). Tableau pivots will reach that BFS; intermediate ratio tests identify leaving variable each pivot.\n\n---\n\n## 42) Lagrange multipliers\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nMinimize \\(f(x)\\) subject to equality \\(g(x)=0\\). Lagrangian:\n$$\n\\mathcal{L}(x,\\lambda)=f(x)\u002B\\lambda^T g(x)\n$$\nStationarity:\n$$\n\\nabla_x \\mathcal{L}=0,\\quad g(x)=0\n$$\n\n### Python implementation (solve KKT for equality constraints)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef lagrange_equalities(grad_f, jac_g, x0, lam0, max_iter=50, tol=1e-12):\n    x = _as_float_array(x0).reshape(-1)\n    lam = _as_float_array(lam0).reshape(-1)\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        g = _as_float_array(jac_g(x)[\u0022g\u0022]).reshape(-1)      # constraint values\n        J = _as_float_array(jac_g(x)[\u0022J\u0022])                  # Jacobian\n        gf = _as_float_array(grad_f(x)).reshape(-1)\n\n        # Solve linearized KKT:\n        # [ I  J^T ][dx] = -[gf \u002B J^T lam]\n        # [ J  0  ][dl]   -[g]\n        K = np.block([[np.eye(len(x)), J.T],\n                      [J, np.zeros((len(g), len(g)))]])\n        rhs = -np.concatenate([gf \u002B J.T @ lam, g])\n        sol = np.linalg.solve(K, rhs)\n        dx = sol[:len(x)]\n        dlam = sol[len(x):]\n        x_new = x \u002B dx\n        lam_new = lam \u002B dlam\n        if np.linalg.norm(dx) \u003C tol and np.linalg.norm(g) \u003C tol:\n            return x_new, lam_new\n        x, lam = x_new, lam_new\n    return x, lam\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nMinimize \\(f(x,y)=x^2\u002By^2\\) s.t. \\(x\u002By-1=0\\).  \n\\(\\mathcal{L}=x^2\u002By^2\u002B\\lambda(x\u002By-1)\\).  \nStationarity: \\(2x\u002B\\lambda=0\\), \\(2y\u002B\\lambda=0\\Rightarrow x=y\\).  \nConstraint: \\(2x=1\\Rightarrow x=y=0.5\\).  \n\\(\\lambda=-1\\).\n\n---\n\n## 43) KKT conditions\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFor inequality constraints \\(g_i(x)\\le0\\), equality \\(h(x)=0\\):  \nLagrangian:\n$$\n\\mathcal{L}=f(x)\u002B\\lambda^T h(x)\u002B\\mu^T g(x)\n$$\nKKT:\n- Stationarity: \\(\\nabla f\u002B\\nabla h^T\\lambda\u002B\\nabla g^T\\mu=0\\)\n- Primal feasibility: \\(h(x)=0,\\ g(x)\\le0\\)\n- Dual feasibility: \\(\\mu\\ge0\\)\n- Complementary slackness: \\(\\mu_i g_i(x)=0\\)\n\n### Python implementation (check KKT residuals)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef kkt_check(x, grad_f, h, J_h, g, J_g, lam, mu, tol=1e-8):\n    x = _as_float_array(x).reshape(-1)\n    lam = _as_float_array(lam).reshape(-1)\n    mu = _as_float_array(mu).reshape(-1)\n    r_station = grad_f(x) \u002B J_h(x).T @ lam \u002B J_g(x).T @ mu\n    r_primal_h = h(x)\n    r_primal_g = g(x)\n    r_dual = np.minimum(mu, 0.0)\n    r_comp = mu * r_primal_g\n    return {\n        \u0022stationarity_inf\u0022: _norm_inf(r_station),\n        \u0022eq_feas_inf\u0022: _norm_inf(r_primal_h),\n        \u0022ineq_max\u0022: float(np.max(r_primal_g)),\n        \u0022dual_neg_min\u0022: float(np.min(r_dual)),\n        \u0022comp_inf\u0022: _norm_inf(r_comp)\n    }\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nFor \\(f=x^2\u002By^2\\), constraint \\(x\u002By\\ge1\\) rewrite \\(g(x,y)=1-x-y\\le0\\).  \nAt \\((0.5,0.5)\\): \\(g=0\\) active; choose \\(\\mu=1\\) gives stationarity \\(2x- \\mu=0\\Rightarrow 1-1=0\\).\n\n---\n\n## 44) Simulated annealing\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nRandomized search with temperature \\(T\\). Accept worse move \\(\\Delta E\u003E0\\) with probability:\n$$\np=\\exp(-\\Delta E/T)\n$$\nReduce \\(T\\) by schedule.\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef simulated_annealing(f, x0, step, T0=1.0, cooling=0.99, iters=5000, seed=0):\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n    x = float(x0)\n    fx = float(f(x))\n    best_x, best_fx = x, fx\n    T = float(T0)\n\n    for _ in range(int(iters)):\n        x_new = x \u002B step * rng.normal()\n        f_new = float(f(x_new))\n        dE = f_new - fx\n        if dE \u003C= 0 or rng.uniform() \u003C np.exp(-dE / max(T, 1e-15)):\n            x, fx = x_new, f_new\n            if fx \u003C best_fx:\n                best_x, best_fx = x, fx\n        T *= cooling\n    return best_x, best_fx\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nMinimize \\(f(x)=x^4-x^2\\). From \\(x_0=0.1\\), propose \\(x_1=0.3\\).  \nCompute \\(\\Delta E=f(0.3)-f(0.1)\\). If \\(\\Delta E\u003E0\\), accept with \\(\\exp(-\\Delta E/T)\\).\n\n---\n\n# Statistics \u0026 Probability\n\n## 45) Bayes’ theorem derivation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nFrom joint probability:\n$$\nP(A\\cap B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A)\n$$\nThus:\n$$\nP(A|B)=\\frac{P(B|A)P(A)}{P(B)}\n$$\nAnd:\n$$\nP(B)=\\sum_i P(B|A_i)P(A_i)\n$$\n(HMM/ML references often use this repeatedly.) [5][9]\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef bayes_posterior(prior_A, likelihood_B_given_A, evidence_B):\n    prior_A = float(prior_A)\n    likelihood_B_given_A = float(likelihood_B_given_A)\n    evidence_B = float(evidence_B)\n    return (likelihood_B_given_A * prior_A) / evidence_B\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nDisease test: \\(P(D)=0.01\\), \\(P(\u002B|D)=0.99\\), \\(P(\u002B|\\neg D)=0.05\\).  \nEvidence:\n\\(P(\u002B)=0.99*0.01\u002B0.05*0.99=0.0099\u002B0.0495=0.0594\\).  \nPosterior:\n\\(P(D|\u002B)=0.99*0.01/0.0594=0.0099/0.0594=0.1667\\).\n\n---\n\n## 46) Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nGiven data \\(x_1,\\dots,x_n\\) with density \\(p(x|\\theta)\\):\n$$\n\\hat{\\theta}=\\arg\\max_\\theta \\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i|\\theta)\n$$\nUse log-likelihood:\n$$\n\\ell(\\theta)=\\sum_{i=1}^n \\log p(x_i|\\theta)\n$$\n\n### Python implementation (Gaussian mean/variance MLE)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef mle_gaussian_params(data):\n    x = _as_float_array(data).reshape(-1)\n    mu_hat = float(np.mean(x))\n    # MLE variance uses 1/n (not unbiased 1/(n-1))\n    sigma2_hat = float(np.mean((x - mu_hat)**2))\n    return mu_hat, sigma2_hat\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nData \\([1,2,4]\\).  \n\\(\\hat\\mu=(1\u002B2\u002B4)/3=7/3=2.3333\\).  \nSquared deviations: \\(( -1.3333)^2=1.7778\\), \\((-0.3333)^2=0.1111\\), \\((1.6667)^2=2.7778\\).  \n\\(\\hat\\sigma^2=(1.7778\u002B0.1111\u002B2.7778)/3=1.5556\\).\n\n---\n\n## 47) Linear regression derivation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nModel \\(y=X\\beta\u002B\\epsilon\\). Least squares:\n$$\n\\hat\\beta=\\arg\\min_\\beta \\|X\\beta-y\\|_2^2\n$$\nNormal equations:\n$$\nX^TX\\hat\\beta=X^Ty\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef linear_regression_fit(X, y):\n    X = _as_float_array(X)\n    y = _as_float_array(y).reshape(-1)\n    beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)\n    return beta\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nFit \\(y\\approx c_0\u002Bc_1x\\) with earlier points: gives \\(c_0=1.1667,c_1=0.5\\) (see LS section intermediates).\n\n---\n\n## 48) Logistic regression\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nBinary \\(y\\in\\{0,1\\}\\):\n$$\nP(y=1|x)=\\sigma(w^Tx)=\\frac{1}{1\u002Be^{-w^Tx}}\n$$\nLog-likelihood:\n$$\n\\ell(w)=\\sum_i \\left[y_i\\log\\sigma(z_i)\u002B(1-y_i)\\log(1-\\sigma(z_i))\\right],\\ z_i=w^Tx_i\n$$\nGradient:\n$$\n\\nabla \\ell(w)=\\sum_i (y_i-\\sigma(z_i))x_i\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef logistic_regression_fit(X, y, lr=0.1, max_iter=5000, tol=1e-8):\n    X = _as_float_array(X)\n    y = _as_float_array(y).reshape(-1)\n    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])\n\n    def sigmoid(z):\n        return 1.0 / (1.0 \u002B np.exp(-z))\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        z = X @ w\n        p = sigmoid(z)\n        g = X.T @ (y - p)\n        w_new = w \u002B lr * g\n        if np.linalg.norm(w_new - w) \u003C tol:\n            return w_new\n        w = w_new\n    return w\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (one gradient step)\nOne feature with intercept: \\(X=[[1,0],[1,1]]\\), \\(y=[0,1]\\), \\(w=(0,0)\\).  \n\\(z=(0,0)\\), \\(p=(0.5,0.5)\\).  \n\\(y-p=(-0.5,0.5)\\).  \nGradient \\(g=X^T(y-p)=(0,0.5)\\).  \nWith lr=1: \\(w=(0,0.5)\\).\n\n---\n\n## 49) PCA derivation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nCentered data matrix \\(X\\). Covariance:\n$$\nC=\\frac{1}{n-1}X^TX\n$$\nPCA directions are eigenvectors of \\(C\\):\n$$\nC v_i=\\lambda_i v_i\n$$\nEquivalently via SVD \\(X=U\\Sigma V^T\\), principal axes \\(V\\), variances \\(\\Sigma^2/(n-1)\\).\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef pca(X, k=None):\n    X = _as_float_array(X)\n    Xc = X - np.mean(X, axis=0, keepdims=True)\n    U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=False)\n    if k is None:\n        k = Vt.shape[0]\n    components = Vt[:k].T\n    explained_var = (s[:k]**2) / (X.shape[0]-1)\n    return components, explained_var\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nPoints \\((1,0),(2,0),(3,0)\\). Centered: \\((-1,0),(0,0),(1,0)\\).  \nCovariance \\(C=\\frac{1}{2}\\begin{bmatrix}2\u00260\\\\0\u00260\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}1\u00260\\\\0\u00260\\end{bmatrix}\\).  \nEigenvectors: first axis \\((1,0)\\) with eigenvalue 1.\n\n---\n\n## 50) k-means derivation\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nMinimize within-cluster SSE:\n$$\nJ=\\sum_{i=1}^n \\|x_i-\\mu_{c_i}\\|^2\n$$\nAlternating minimization:\n1) Assign \\(c_i=\\arg\\min_k \\|x_i-\\mu_k\\|^2\\)  \n2) Update \\(\\mu_k=\\frac{1}{|C_k|}\\sum_{i\\in C_k} x_i\\)\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef kmeans(X, k, max_iter=100, seed=0):\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n    X = _as_float_array(X)\n    n = X.shape[0]\n    centers = X[rng.choice(n, k, replace=False)]\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        d2 = ((X[:, None, :] - centers[None, :, :])**2).sum(axis=2)\n        labels = np.argmin(d2, axis=1)\n        new_centers = np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) for j in range(k)])\n        if np.linalg.norm(new_centers - centers) \u003C 1e-10:\n            break\n        centers = new_centers\n    return centers, labels\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\nPoints \\(\\{0,2,8,10\\}\\) in 1D, \\(k=2\\). Start centers \\(0,10\\).  \nAssign: \\(\\{0,2\\}\\to0\\), \\(\\{8,10\\}\\to10\\).  \nUpdate: \\(\\mu_1=1\\), \\(\\mu_2=9\\). Next assignment unchanged → converged.\n\n---\n\n## 51) Gaussian mixture models (GMM)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nMixture:\n$$\np(x)=\\sum_{k=1}^K \\pi_k \\mathcal{N}(x|\\mu_k,\\Sigma_k)\n$$\nEM: responsibilities\n$$\n\\gamma_{ik}=\\frac{\\pi_k \\mathcal{N}(x_i|\\mu_k,\\Sigma_k)}{\\sum_j \\pi_j \\mathcal{N}(x_i|\\mu_j,\\Sigma_j)}\n$$\nM-step:\n$$\nN_k=\\sum_i\\gamma_{ik},\\quad \\pi_k=N_k/n,\\quad\n\\mu_k=\\frac{1}{N_k}\\sum_i \\gamma_{ik}x_i\n$$\n$$\n\\Sigma_k=\\frac{1}{N_k}\\sum_i \\gamma_{ik}(x_i-\\mu_k)(x_i-\\mu_k)^T\n$$\n\n### Python implementation (full-cov, small K)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef gmm_em(X, K, max_iter=100, seed=0, eps=1e-6):\n    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)\n    X = _as_float_array(X)\n    n, d = X.shape\n    mu = X[rng.choice(n, K, replace=False)]\n    Sigma = np.array([np.eye(d) for _ in range(K)])\n    pi = np.ones(K) / K\n\n    def gauss_pdf(x, m, S):\n        S = S \u002B eps*np.eye(d)\n        det = np.linalg.det(S)\n        inv = np.linalg.inv(S)\n        diff = x - m\n        expo = -0.5 * diff.T @ inv @ diff\n        norm = 1.0 / np.sqrt((2*np.pi)**d * det)\n        return float(norm * np.exp(expo))\n\n    for _ in range(max_iter):\n        gamma = np.zeros((n, K))\n        for i in range(n):\n            denom = 0.0\n            for k in range(K):\n                gamma[i, k] = pi[k] * gauss_pdf(X[i], mu[k], Sigma[k])\n                denom \u002B= gamma[i, k]\n            gamma[i, :] /= max(denom, 1e-15)\n\n        Nk = np.sum(gamma, axis=0)\n        pi = Nk / n\n        for k in range(K):\n            mu[k] = (gamma[:, k][:, None] * X).sum(axis=0) / max(Nk[k], 1e-15)\n            diff = X - mu[k]\n            Sigma[k] = (gamma[:, k][:, None, None] * (diff[:, :, None] @ diff[:, None, :])).sum(axis=0) / max(Nk[k], 1e-15)\n    return pi, mu, Sigma\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (one E-step)\n1D points \\(x=[0,1,9,10]\\), \\(K=2\\), init \\(\\mu=[0,10]\\), \\(\\sigma^2=1\\), \\(\\pi=0.5\\).  \nCompute \\(\\gamma_{i1}\\) using Gaussian pdf at each point; e.g. for \\(x=1\\): pdf near \\(\\mu=0\\) is high, near 10 is tiny → \\(\\gamma\\approx1\\) for cluster1.\n\n---\n\n## 52) Markov chains\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nTransition matrix \\(P\\), \\(P_{ij}=P(X_{t\u002B1}=j|X_t=i)\\).  \nState distribution evolves:\n$$\n\\pi_{t\u002B1}=\\pi_t P\n$$\nStationary distribution:\n$$\n\\pi=\\pi P,\\quad \\sum_i \\pi_i=1\n$$\n\n### Python implementation\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef markov_step(pi, P):\n    pi = _as_float_array(pi).reshape(-1)\n    P = _as_float_array(P)\n    return pi @ P\n\ndef stationary_distribution(P, iters=10000, tol=1e-12):\n    P = _as_float_array(P)\n    n = P.shape[0]\n    pi = np.ones(n) / n\n    for _ in range(iters):\n        pi_new = pi @ P\n        if _norm_inf(pi_new - pi) \u003C tol:\n            return pi_new\n        pi = pi_new\n    return pi\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example\n\\(P=\\begin{bmatrix}0.9\u00260.1\\\\0.2\u00260.8\\end{bmatrix}\\), start \\(\\pi_0=(1,0)\\).  \n\\(\\pi_1=(0.9,0.1)\\).  \n\\(\\pi_2=(0.9,0.1)P=(0.9*0.9\u002B0.1*0.2,\\;0.9*0.1\u002B0.1*0.8)=(0.83,0.17)\\).  \nStationary solves \\(\\pi=\\pi P\\Rightarrow \\pi=(2/3,1/3)\\).\n\n---\n\n## 53) Hidden Markov Models (HMMs)\n\n### Mathematical foundation\nHMM parameters: initial \\(\\pi\\), transition \\(A\\), emissions \\(B\\). [9][5][10]  \nForward probabilities:\n$$\n\\alpha_1(i)=\\pi_i b_i(o_1)\n$$\n$$\n\\alpha_{t\u002B1}(j)=\\left(\\sum_i \\alpha_t(i)a_{ij}\\right)b_j(o_{t\u002B1})\n$$\nViterbi (most likely path):\n$$\n\\delta_{t\u002B1}(j)=\\max_i \\delta_t(i)a_{ij}\\, b_j(o_{t\u002B1})\n$$\n\n### Python implementation (discrete emissions)\n\u0060\u0060\u0060python\ndef hmm_forward(pi, A, B, obs):\n    pi = _as_float_array(pi); A = _as_float_array(A); B = _as_float_array(B)\n    obs = list(obs)\n    N = len(pi); T = len(obs)\n    alpha = np.zeros((T, N))\n    alpha[0] = pi * B[:, obs[0]]\n    for t in range(T-1):\n        alpha[t\u002B1] = (alpha[t] @ A) * B[:, obs[t\u002B1]]\n    return alpha, float(np.sum(alpha[-1]))\n\ndef hmm_viterbi(pi, A, B, obs):\n    pi = _as_float_array(pi); A = _as_float_array(A); B = _as_float_array(B)\n    obs = list(obs)\n    N = len(pi); T = len(obs)\n    delta = np.zeros((T, N))\n    psi = np.zeros((T, N), dtype=int)\n\n    delta[0] = pi * B[:, obs[0]]\n    for t in range(1, T):\n        for j in range(N):\n            vals = delta[t-1] * A[:, j]\n            psi[t, j] = int(np.argmax(vals))\n            delta[t, j] = np.max(vals) * B[j, obs[t]]\n\n    path = np.zeros(T, dtype=int)\n    path[-1] = int(np.argmax(delta[-1]))\n    for t in range(T-2, -1, -1):\n        path[t] = psi[t\u002B1, path[t\u002B1]]\n    return path, float(np.max(delta[-1]))\n\u0060\u0060\u0060\n\n### Worked example (forward intermediates)\nTwo states \\(S=\\{0,1\\}\\), observations \\(\\{0,1\\}\\).  \n\\(\\pi=(0.6,0.4)\\).  \n\\(A=\\begin{bmatrix}0.7\u00260.3\\\\0.4\u00260.6\\end{bmatrix}\\).  \n\\(B=\\begin{bmatrix}0.5\u00260.5\\\\0.1\u00260.9\\end{bmatrix}\\).  \nObs sequence \\(o=[1,0]\\).  \n\\(\\alpha_1=(0.6*0.5,\\;0.4*0.9)=(0.3,0.36)\\).  \nNext:\n\\(\\alpha_2(0)=((0.3*0.7\u002B0.36*0.4))*0.5=(0.21\u002B0.144)*0.5=0.177\\).  \n\\(\\alpha_2(1)=((0.3*0.3\u002B0.36*0.6))*0.1=(0.09\u002B0.216)*0.1=0.0306\\).  \nLikelihood \\(P(o)=0.2076\\).\n\n---\n\n# Quick “What you can do next”\nIf you tell me **your preferred formatting target** (Markdown doc, Word, or internal wiki style), I can restructure this into a ready-to-paste **knowledge base layout** (navigation, cross-links, consistent notation), while keeping the same math/code and the same topic order.\n\n[1]: https://www.press.jhu.edu/books/title/10678/matrix-computations \u0022Matrix Computations | Hopkins Press\u0022\n[2]: https://books.google.com/books/about/Numerical_Analysis.html?id=75PBQgAACAAJ \u0022Numerical Analysis - Richard L.
